plain: A tax-free swap of one life policy or annuity for another, named after the tax code section that allows it.
snappy: A tax-free transfer of cash value from one life policy or annuity into another, preserving the original cost basis.
detail: A 1035 exchange lets you move the cash value of an old life policy or annuity into a better one without triggering tax on the gains, as long as the money goes directly between insurers. People use it to escape an underperforming policy, lower costs, or shift into an annuity for income. The original cost basis carries over. Done wrong — by taking the cash yourself first — it becomes a taxable surrender.

plain: A feature letting a terminally ill policyholder collect part of their life insurance early.
snappy: A rider letting an insured with a terminal or chronic illness draw part of the death benefit while still alive.
detail: An accelerated death benefit rider lets someone facing a terminal diagnosis, or sometimes a chronic or critical illness, tap a portion of the death benefit early to pay for care or final wishes. Whatever is advanced is subtracted from what beneficiaries later receive. Often included free on modern policies, it has eased the case for life insurance as more than a post-death payout, blurring into long-term care coverage.

plain: A feature that stops your first at-fault crash from raising your premium.
snappy: A benefit waiving the premium surcharge for a driver's first at-fault accident, usually earned through a clean record.
detail: Accident forgiveness spares you the surcharge after your first at-fault crash, so a single mistake doesn't spike your premium for years. Insurers grant it to drivers with a long clean record or sell it as an add-on. The fine print matters: it usually applies to one accident, may not transfer if you switch carriers, and doesn't erase the accident from your record — it just shields the rate.

plain: Extra life insurance money paid if you die in an accident rather than from illness.
snappy: A rider paying an additional death benefit, often double the face amount, when death results from a covered accident.
detail: The accidental death benefit rider — the old "double indemnity" of film noir — pays beneficiaries extra, often twice the face amount, if the insured dies in a qualifying accident. It's cheap because accidental deaths are rare, but the exclusions are broad (no payout for many illness-linked or risky-activity deaths), so insurers seldom pay. Advisers generally call it poor value versus simply buying more base coverage.

plain: A team of doctors and hospitals that shares in the savings if it keeps a group of patients healthy for less.
snappy: A provider group held jointly accountable for the cost and quality of a defined patient population, sharing in savings.
detail: An accountable care organization is a network of providers that agrees to manage a population's care and split the savings with the payer if it beats a cost target while hitting quality marks — and sometimes shares the losses if it doesn't. Medicare pioneered the model to push value-based care. It nudges hospitals and doctors to coordinate rather than each bill in isolation, the opposite of fee-for-service.

plain: The years a deferred annuity grows your money before you start taking income.
snappy: The period when the value of an annuity builds through premiums and tax-deferred growth, before payout begins.
detail: The accumulation phase is the saving stage of a deferred annuity: premiums go in and the value compounds tax-deferred, untouched by income payments. How it grows — a fixed rate, an index, or invested subaccounts — defines the annuity type. Surrender charges discourage early withdrawals during this phase. It ends when the owner annuitizes or starts withdrawals, flipping into the payout phase.

plain: What damaged property was worth at the moment it was lost — its replacement cost minus wear and tear.
snappy: A settlement basis equal to replacement cost minus depreciation, paying what the property was actually worth when lost.
detail: Total your ten-year-old roof and an actual cash value policy pays for a ten-year-old roof, not a new one — replacement cost less depreciation. It's cheaper to buy but leaves a gap you cover out of pocket. Many homeowners later wish they'd paid more for replacement cost coverage, especially on roofs, where insurers increasingly impose actual cash value to limit their payouts.

plain: The share of medical costs a health plan covers on average — the math behind the metal tiers.
snappy: The percentage of total covered costs a plan pays on average for a standard population, fixing its metal tier.
detail: A plan with 70% actuarial value — a silver plan — pays roughly 70% of a typical population's covered costs, leaving 30% to deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. It's an average across many people, not a promise for any one person. Actuaries compute it to slot plans into metal tiers so buyers can compare generosity at a glance. It's where insurance pricing meets the ACA's consumer-protection rules.

plain: Someone added to your policy so they're protected too — often a landlord or business partner who demands it.
snappy: A party other than the named insured granted coverage under the policy, usually by endorsement to satisfy a contract.
detail: Landlords, lenders, and clients routinely require that they be named on a tenant's or contractor's liability policy, so that it responds if they're sued over the work. The status is added by endorsement and usually doesn't raise the limit — the added party shares the coverage of the named insured. Construction contracts live and die on whether this language was drafted correctly.

plain: Home insurance that pays your extra costs — hotels, meals — when a covered disaster forces you out of your house.
snappy: The homeowners coverage paying the extra cost of living elsewhere while a damaged home is repaired.
detail: If a fire makes your home unlivable, additional living expenses, the homeowners form of loss of use, pays the gap between your normal costs and the pricier reality of a hotel, restaurant meals, and storage while the house is rebuilt. It covers only the increase, not your whole budget, and runs up against time or dollar caps. Keeping receipts during displacement is how families actually collect it.

plain: The 2010 health law that created online marketplaces, subsidies, and rules banning denial for pre-existing conditions.
snappy: The 2010 law overhauling US health coverage with marketplaces, premium subsidies, and guaranteed-issue protections.
detail: The Affordable Care Act reshaped individual health insurance: it set up the marketplaces where people buy subsidised plans, barred insurers from rejecting or surcharging pre-existing conditions, required plans to cover essential health benefits with no lifetime limits, and capped the out-of-pocket maximum. Premium tax credits make coverage affordable for many. It remains the backbone of how the uninsured and self-employed get covered, and a perennial political fight.

plain: Replacement car parts made by someone other than the original manufacturer, usually cheaper.
snappy: Repair parts produced by third parties rather than the vehicle's maker, often used to lower claim costs.
detail: Aftermarket parts are made by companies other than the carmaker and typically cost less than OEM parts, so insurers favour them to hold down repair bills, especially on older vehicles. Quality ranges from equivalent to inferior, which fuels disputes over fit and safety. Some states require insurers to disclose their use and let owners pay the difference for OEM parts. Body shops and owners often push back when a policy mandates them.

plain: The total an insurer will pay over the whole policy term, across all claims combined.
snappy: The maximum a policy pays for all covered losses during its term, separate from the per-occurrence limit on each event.
detail: A general liability policy might carry a $1 million per-occurrence limit and a $2 million aggregate: any one claim is capped at a million, and once total payouts reach two million the policy is exhausted for the year. A string of claims can burn through the aggregate and leave you bare before renewal. Knowing how much aggregate is left is vital when a second loss follows a first.

plain: A property policy where the insurer accepts a set value up front, so no coinsurance penalty can cut your claim.
snappy: A commercial property option that suspends the coinsurance clause by fixing an agreed insurable value at the start of the term.
detail: Agreed value is the escape hatch from a coinsurance penalty: the business and insurer agree on the property's insurable value when the policy is written, usually backed by a signed statement of values, and the coinsurance clause is switched off. A covered total loss then pays the full limit with no penalty for under-insuring. It costs more than a standard coinsurance form, but it removes the nasty surprise of a reduced payout discovered only after a fire.

plain: The price your plan has decided a service is worth — the basis for what it and you actually pay.
snappy: The maximum a plan recognises as payable for a covered service; the negotiated rate on which cost-sharing is figured.
detail: The doctor may charge $300, but if your plan's allowed amount is $180, that's the number that matters: the plan pays its share of $180 and your coinsurance is figured on it. In-network providers write off the rest; out-of-network ones can bill you for it. The allowed amount appears on every explanation of benefits as the line between billed and covered.

plain: The person an annuity bases its lifetime payments on.
snappy: The individual whose age and life expectancy an annuity uses to size its payout, often but not always the owner.
detail: The annuitant is to an annuity what the insured is to life insurance: lifetime payments are calculated on this person's age and life expectancy. Usually they also own the contract, but the two roles can differ. When a lifetime annuity is annuitized, the size of each cheque depends directly on how long they are expected to live.

plain: Flipping an annuity from a savings pot into a guaranteed stream of income payments.
snappy: Converting the accumulated value of an annuity into a series of periodic income payments, often guaranteed for life.
detail: Annuitization is the switch that turns the money in a deferred annuity into income: you give up access to the lump sum in exchange for regular payments, typically for life or a set period. It's irreversible, which is both its strength — guaranteed income you can't outlive — and its drawback — no lump sum left for heirs unless you add a period-certain or refund feature. Many owners never annuitize, withdrawing instead.

plain: A contract with an insurer that turns a lump sum into a stream of income, often for life.
snappy: An insurance contract that, in exchange for a premium, pays a stream of income, immediately or starting later.
detail: An annuity is life insurance run backwards: instead of paying when you die, it pays while you live, protecting against outliving your money. You hand an insurer a lump sum or a series of premiums; it returns income now (an immediate annuity) or later (a deferred annuity), for a set period or for life. Retirees buy them for a private pension; critics flag high fees and surrender charges on complex versions.

plain: Your formal request asking the plan to reconsider after it denies a claim or service.
snappy: A challenge by the policyholder to a coverage denial, first reviewed internally and then, if needed, by an outside reviewer.
detail: When a plan denies a claim or refuses to authorise care, you have the right to appeal — first an internal review by the plan, then an external review by an independent third party whose decision the ACA makes binding. Many denials are overturned on appeal, yet most patients never file. Knowing the deadlines and attaching the doctor's supporting letter is how a wrongly denied claim gets paid.

plain: The form where you tell the insurer about yourself so it can decide whether and how to cover you.
snappy: The form on which a prospective insured discloses the facts underwriters use to accept, price, or decline the risk.
detail: The application is the foundation of utmost good faith: answer honestly, because a material misrepresentation here can let the insurer rescind the policy and refuse a claim later. Underwriters lean on it to classify the risk and set the premium. For life and disability cover the application may trigger a medical exam and a check of prescription and claims databases before an offer is made.

plain: A policy provision for settling a disagreement over how much a damaged car or home is worth.
snappy: A clause letting insurer and insured each hire an appraiser, with an umpire deciding, to resolve a dispute over loss value.
detail: When you and the insurer can't agree on the value of a total loss or repair, the appraisal clause offers a way out short of court: each side hires an independent appraiser, and the two pick an umpire to break any tie, with the result binding on the amount. It resolves how much, not whether something is covered. Common in auto and homeowners policies, it's an underused tool for owners who think a payout is too low.

plain: The insurer-of-last-resort pool that covers drivers no company will voluntarily insure.
snappy: A state mechanism distributing drivers who can't buy voluntary coverage among insurers, guaranteeing minimum access.
detail: When no insurer will voluntarily cover a high-risk driver, a state assigned-risk plan steps in: applicants are parcelled out among all insurers doing business there, who must take their share. It guarantees that everyone legally required to carry insurance can buy at least the minimum — at a high price. It's the auto version of a residual market, the safety net beneath the nonstandard market.

plain: A crash the insurer decides you primarily caused, which usually raises your premium.
snappy: An accident an insurer assigns chiefly to its insured, typically triggering a surcharge or higher renewal premium.
detail: When the insurer decides you were primarily to blame for a crash, it's an at-fault accident — and the consequences follow you: a surcharge, a lost safe-driver discount, or a higher premium for years. Insurers weigh police reports, statements, and damage patterns to assign fault. Accident-forgiveness features can spare a first at-fault accident. Comparative-negligence rules can split fault between drivers, softening the hit.

plain: A report from your own doctor the life insurer requests to confirm your medical history.
snappy: A record an insurer obtains from an applicant's physician to verify medical history during life or disability underwriting.
detail: When an application or exam raises questions, the underwriter orders an attending physician statement — your doctor's records — to confirm diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes before deciding. It's the most thorough and slowest step, often delaying a decision by weeks while the records arrive. Applicants sign a medical-records authorisation allowing the request. It's why full underwriting takes longer than simplified issue, which skips it.

plain: A hazard that lures children — a pool, a trampoline — making the owner liable even for trespassers.
snappy: A doctrine holding owners liable for child injuries from tempting hazards like pools, even when the child trespasses.
detail: The attractive nuisance doctrine makes a property owner responsible for injuries to children drawn in by a dangerous temptation — most famously a swimming pool, but also a trampoline, an old refrigerator, or construction equipment — even if the child was trespassing. It overrides the usual lower duty owed to trespassers. It's why insurers surcharge or restrict coverage for pools and trampolines, the classic attractive nuisances that drive homeowner liability claims.

plain: Coverage for your car that pays for crashes, theft, and the harm you cause others while driving.
snappy: Coverage for vehicles bundling liability for others' losses with optional collision and comprehensive for your own car.
detail: Auto insurance is mandatory almost everywhere you drive, combining liability coverage that pays for injury and damage you cause others with optional collision and comprehensive coverage for your own vehicle. Premiums hinge on your driving record, location, vehicle, and often a credit-based insurance score. Lenders require collision and comprehensive while a loan is outstanding. It's the policy most people buy first and shop most often as rates climb.

plain: Coverage for aircraft and the liability of flying them — from a single private plane to an airline fleet.
snappy: Coverage for physical damage to aircraft (hull) and liability for passenger injury and ground damage arising from their operation.
detail: Aviation insurance covers two things: hull damage to the aircraft itself, and the liability for injuries to passengers or people and property on the ground. It spans a weekend pilot's single-engine plane up to an airline's fleet, with premiums driven by the aircraft, its use, and the pilot's hours. Because a single crash can produce catastrophic, headline losses, much of the risk is spread to reinsurers and the specialist markets at Lloyd's.

plain: When an insurer treats you unfairly — denying or dragging out a valid claim — and can be punished for it.
snappy: Unreasonable handling of a claim or defence by an insurer, exposing it to damages beyond the policy limit.
detail: Insurers owe their policyholders good faith and fair dealing. Deny a clearly covered claim, lowball a settlement, or refuse to defend without grounds and the insured can sue for bad faith, recovering not just the claim but extra-contractual and sometimes punitive damages. The threat keeps carriers honest and is why a reasonable but wrong denial is defensible while an arbitrary one is dangerous.

plain: When an out-of-network provider bills you for the gap between their charge and what your plan paid.
snappy: Charging a patient the difference between a provider's full charge and the plan's allowed amount, common out-of-network.
detail: Balance billing hits when an out-of-network provider charges $1,000, the plan's allowed amount is $400, and you're billed the $600 gap on top of your cost-share. It produced the notorious surprise bills from out-of-network emergency-room doctors at in-network hospitals. The No Surprises Act now bars it in many of those situations, but it still applies when you knowingly choose an out-of-network provider.

plain: The person who collects the money when a life insurance policy pays out.
snappy: The person or entity designated to receive the proceeds of a life insurance policy or annuity when the insured dies.
detail: You name a beneficiary when you buy life insurance — a spouse, child, trust, or charity. Primary beneficiaries get paid first; contingent ones inherit only if the primary has died. Keeping the designation current is critical: proceeds go to whoever is named on the form, not whoever a will lists, which is why divorces and remarriages trigger so many disputed payouts. The named beneficiary generally takes the money free of income tax.

plain: A deduction insurers make when a repair leaves your car better than before the loss.
snappy: A reduction in a claim payment reflecting the added value when worn parts are replaced with new ones during repair.
detail: If a crash forces replacing a half-worn tyre or an ageing battery with a new one, the insurer may apply a betterment deduction, asking you to chip in for the upgrade since you ended up better off than before. The indemnity principle — restoring you to your pre-loss position, not improving it — is the logic. It surfaces most on wear-prone parts and is a common line-item dispute at the body shop.

plain: Temporary proof you're covered right now, before the full policy paperwork arrives.
snappy: A short-term agreement providing immediate coverage while the formal policy is being written and issued.
detail: When you buy a car at noon, the agent issues a binder so you can legally drive it home before the printed policy exists. A binder carries the same coverage as the policy it stands in for, but only for a set period — often 30 to 90 days — until the real document is issued or declined. Lenders accept a binder as proof of insurance at a closing.

plain: One shared limit covering several buildings or property types at once, instead of a separate limit on each.
snappy: A commercial property option applying a single limit across multiple locations or categories, giving claims flexibility.
detail: Blanket coverage pools one limit over several insured items — multiple buildings, contents at many sites, or both — rather than boxing each into its own sub-limit. After a loss, the full blanket limit is available wherever the damage falls, so a business that under-stated one location isn't capped there. It suits companies whose values shift between sites, like retailers moving inventory, and usually rides alongside an agreed-value or high coinsurance requirement.

plain: The car insurance that pays the medical bills and lost wages of people you injure in a crash.
snappy: Auto liability coverage paying others' medical costs, lost income, and pain-and-suffering claims when the insured is at fault.
detail: Bodily injury liability covers the human cost of an at-fault crash — the other driver's and passengers' medical bills, lost wages, and pain-and-suffering claims, plus your legal defence. It's the first number in a split-limit policy, like the 25 and 50 in 25/50/25 (per-person and per-accident caps). Because injury awards can run into millions, low state-minimum limits are the biggest gap most drivers don't realise they have.

plain: Coverage for a building while it's under construction, protecting the structure and materials on site.
snappy: Property coverage during construction or renovation, insuring the structure, materials, and equipment against loss on site.
detail: A house under construction isn't a finished home, so it needs builders risk insurance — course-of-construction coverage — protecting the rising structure, materials, and sometimes equipment against fire, theft, and weather until the project is done. The owner, builder, or developer carries it, and it ends when the building is complete and occupied, handing off to a standard property policy. Lenders financing construction require it.

plain: Coverage that replaces the profit a business loses while it's shut down repairing covered damage.
snappy: Coverage for lost net income and continuing expenses while operations are suspended by covered physical damage.
detail: Business income insurance, often called business interruption, pays the earnings a company would have made had a fire or storm not closed its doors. It covers lost net profit plus the bills that grind on — payroll, rent, loan payments — during the restoration period, until the business reopens. The pandemic exposed how tightly it's tied to physical damage, since most policies require a covered physical loss to trigger. It's frequently the coverage that decides whether a damaged business survives.

plain: The movable things a business owns — furniture, equipment, inventory — as opposed to the building itself.
snappy: The category of commercial property coverage for a company's contents: furniture, fixtures, machinery, stock, and equipment.
detail: Business personal property is the contents half of a commercial property policy: everything a company owns that isn't the building — desks, computers, tools, shelving, and the inventory waiting to be sold. A tenant who rents space insures business personal property even when the landlord covers the structure. Setting its limit means tallying what it would cost to replace the whole operation's gear, a figure owners routinely underestimate until a fire forces the count.

plain: A bundled small-business policy — property plus liability in one package at a friendly price.
snappy: A packaged policy combining commercial property and general liability coverage, designed for small and mid-sized businesses.
detail: A businessowners policy is the small-business equivalent of a homeowners package: it folds commercial property, general liability, and business income into one pre-built, discounted bundle aimed at low-to-moderate-risk firms like shops, offices, and restaurants. It simplifies buying and usually costs less than the same coverages bought separately. Businesses that outgrow its eligibility or need bespoke terms graduate to a commercial package policy assembled coverage by coverage.

plain: A workplace benefits menu that lets you pay for health coverage and other perks with pre-tax dollars.
snappy: An employer benefit plan under tax code Section 125 letting employees choose benefits and pay with pre-tax salary.
detail: A cafeteria plan, named for its pick-and-choose menu, lets workers fund health premiums, a flexible spending account, or dependent care with pre-tax salary, cutting their taxable income. It's the tax plumbing behind most employer benefit enrollments. The Section 125 rules govern what can be offered and when elections can change — which is why mid-year benefit changes usually require a qualifying life event.

plain: Ending a policy before its term is up — by you or the insurer.
snappy: Termination of a policy before its expiration date, by the insured or, for limited reasons, by the insurer.
detail: You can usually cancel anytime and get back the unused premium. An insurer's power to cancel mid-term is tightly limited by state law — typically only for non-payment, fraud, or a big rise in the risk — because pulling coverage out from under someone is drastic. After a short initial window, most policies can't be cancelled for ordinary claims; the insurer must wait and nonrenew instead.

plain: Paying a doctor a fixed monthly amount per patient instead of per service.
snappy: A payment model paying providers a set amount per enrolled patient per period, regardless of services actually used.
detail: Under capitation, a plan pays a primary care physician a flat monthly fee for each assigned patient, whether that patient is seen ten times or never. It flips the incentive of fee-for-service: the provider profits by keeping patients healthy and avoiding unnecessary care, but bears the risk if they get sick. Common in HMOs and accountable care arrangements, it's central to the shift toward value-based care.

plain: Coverage for goods while they're being shipped, so a loss in transit doesn't fall on the buyer or seller.
snappy: Coverage protecting freight against loss or damage while in transit by sea, air, road, or rail.
detail: Cargo insurance protects the value of goods on the move — a shipping container of electronics, a truckload of produce across three states. It pays when freight is damaged, stolen, or lost in transit, and contracts of sale spell out which party, buyer or seller, must carry it at each leg. Importers treat it as routine, since a carrier's own liability is usually capped far below the goods' real worth.

plain: What you actually pocket if you cancel a permanent life policy — its cash value minus any surrender charge.
snappy: The amount a policyholder receives on surrendering permanent life insurance: cash value less surrender charges and loans.
detail: Cancel a whole or universal life policy and the insurer pays the cash surrender value — the accumulated cash value reduced by any surrender charge and outstanding policy loans. In the early years surrender charges can wipe out most of it, which is why surrendering soon after buying is costly. Gains above the premiums you paid are taxable. A 1035 exchange can move the value into a new policy or annuity without triggering that tax.

plain: The savings pot inside a permanent life policy that grows over time and that you can borrow or cash out.
snappy: The savings component of permanent life insurance that grows tax-deferred and can be borrowed against or surrendered.
detail: Cash value is what separates permanent life insurance from term: part of each premium builds a tax-deferred account you can borrow against via a policy loan, use to pay premiums, or take by surrendering the policy. Whole life grows it on a guaranteed schedule; universal and variable policies tie it to interest or investments. Borrowing or surrendering reduces the death benefit, and a surrender charge can bite in the early years.

plain: A bare-bones, low-premium health plan for young or low-income people that mainly guards against disaster.
snappy: A low-premium, high-deductible ACA plan, limited to those under 30 or with a hardship exemption, covering worst-case costs.
detail: A catastrophic plan carries the lowest premium and a deductible near the out-of-pocket maximum, so it pays little until a serious illness or accident. It still covers essential health benefits and a few preventive visits and primary-care visits. Only people under 30 or those with a hardship exemption can buy one, and premium tax credits don't apply, which limits its appeal to the young and healthy.

plain: A one-page proof that a business actually carries the coverage it claims, handed to clients and landlords.
snappy: A standardized document summarizing a policyholder's coverage types, limits, and dates as evidence of insurance to a third party.
detail: A certificate of insurance is the receipt that proves coverage exists: a general contractor demands one from every subcontractor, a landlord from every tenant, a venue from every vendor. It lists the policy types, limits, effective dates, and any additional insured status, but it grants no coverage itself — it only reports it. Reading one carefully, and confirming it's current, is how businesses verify the partners they work with are actually insured.

plain: Low-cost government health coverage for kids in families that earn too much for Medicaid but can't easily afford private plans.
snappy: A federal-state program covering children in families above Medicaid limits but below private-coverage affordability.
detail: CHIP fills the gap just above Medicaid eligibility, covering checkups, immunisations, dental, and hospital care for children at low or no cost. States run it alongside Medicaid, sometimes as an extension of it. It enjoys rare bipartisan support and covers millions of kids whose parents earn modestly. Families often discover it when they apply for Medicaid and the children qualify even if the adults don't.

plain: A formal request asking your insurer to pay for a loss the policy covers.
snappy: A demand by the insured (or a third party) for payment under the policy after a covered loss occurs.
detail: Filing a claim starts the payout process: you report the loss, an adjuster investigates, and the insurer pays, partly pays, or denies. Filing too many makes your premium rise or renewal harder. The word also means the eventual cost an insurer bears: "claims came in higher than expected this quarter" is the line that sinks an insurance stock when catastrophes strike.

plain: Whoever is asking the insurer to pay — you, or the person you injured.
snappy: The party making a claim for payment, whether the policyholder (first-party) or an injured outsider (third-party).
detail: In a first-party claim the claimant is the insured asking their own carrier to pay, as when you report a stolen laptop. In a third-party claim the claimant is the outsider you harmed — the driver you rear-ended files against your liability coverage. Adjusters separate the two because their duties differ: they owe good faith to their own insured, and only fair dealing to a third-party claimant.

plain: Liability cover that only pays if the claim is reported while the policy is active.
snappy: A liability policy that responds only to claims first made and reported during its term, often with a retroactive date.
detail: Doctors and professionals usually carry claims-made coverage: it's cheaper at first but the trigger is when the claim is filed, not when the mistake happened. Let the policy end and an old error becomes uninsured unless you buy tail coverage. A retroactive date sets how far back covered acts can reach. Switching carriers requires careful handling so no period falls through the gap.

plain: A numbered category that groups a business's jobs by hazard, setting the base rate for its workers'-comp premium.
snappy: A classification number assigning a type of work to a risk group, used to set workers' compensation and other commercial rates.
detail: Class codes sort the working world by hazard: roofers and loggers sit in expensive codes, clerical staff in cheap ones, and each carries a rate per $100 of payroll. A business's workers'-comp premium starts by multiplying payroll in each class code by that rate, before the experience modification factor adjusts it. Getting employees assigned to the right code matters — a misclassification can swing the bill by thousands, in either direction.

plain: Specialty coverage for collectible vehicles based on an agreed value, with limited annual mileage.
snappy: Coverage for collector vehicles using an agreed value rather than actual cash value, usually capping annual mileage.
detail: A restored 1960s muscle car isn't worth the depreciated value a standard policy would pay, so classic car insurance uses an agreed value set upfront, guaranteeing that amount on a total loss. Premiums are surprisingly low because these cars are driven little and garaged carefully — coverage typically caps annual mileage and bars daily commuting. Specialty insurers dominate the niche, prizing the low-risk way collectors use their vehicles.

plain: A shared database of past insurance claims that insurers check when pricing your home or auto coverage.
snappy: An industry database of a property's and person's prior insurance claims, used to underwrite and price new coverage.
detail: Insurers report and check the CLUE report, a seven-year history of claims tied to a property and a person. A house with a string of water claims, or a buyer with a claims-heavy past, can face higher premiums or a decline even before anything goes wrong. Buyers can request a property's CLUE report before purchase, and consumers can dispute errors much like a credit file.

plain: A law letting you keep your job's health plan for a while after you leave — but you pay the full premium.
snappy: A federal law letting workers and families continue group coverage after job loss, at their own full cost plus a fee.
detail: Lose or leave a job and COBRA lets you keep the same group health plan, usually for up to 18 months — but now you pay the entire premium the employer used to subsidise, plus a 2% fee, so the sticker shock is real. It bridges the gap until new coverage or a special enrollment period. Many people compare the COBRA cost with a marketplace plan and find the subsidised marketplace cheaper.

plain: The share of a covered bill you keep paying even after the deductible — often a percentage.
snappy: A cost-sharing percentage the insured pays after the deductible; in property, a clause penalising under-insurance.
detail: In health insurance, 20% coinsurance means after your deductible you pay a fifth of each bill until you hit the out-of-pocket maximum. In property insurance the word means something different: a coinsurance clause requires you to insure a building to a set percentage of its value (often 80%) or the insurer pays only part of even a small loss. Same word, two traps for the unwary.

plain: A property-policy rule that penalizes you at claim time if you insured the building for too little.
snappy: A commercial property provision requiring coverage to equal a set percentage of value, cutting claim payments if it falls short.
detail: The commercial coinsurance clause is a discipline device: insure the property for at least a stated share of its value — commonly 80%, 90%, or 100% — or the insurer pays only the proportion you carried. Insure a $1 million building for $600,000 under an 80% clause and even a partial loss is paid at three-quarters. It's a different beast from health-plan coinsurance, and it's why setting an accurate insurable value matters so much in property cover.

plain: The part of car insurance that pays to fix your own car after a crash, no matter who's at fault.
snappy: First-party coverage paying to repair or replace the covered vehicle after a collision, subject to a deductible.
detail: Collision coverage repairs your own car after you hit another vehicle or object or roll over, regardless of fault, after you pay the deductible. Lenders require it while a loan or lease is outstanding. On an older car whose value has fallen, drivers often drop it once the premium approaches the payout a total loss would bring. It pairs with comprehensive coverage as the "full coverage" most people picture.

plain: One pooled liability limit covering injuries and property damage together, instead of separate caps.
snappy: A single liability limit applied flexibly across bodily injury and property damage in one accident, rather than split caps.
detail: A combined single limit gives one number — say $300,000 — that can flow to injuries, property damage, or both in any mix for a single accident, rather than the rigid buckets of split limits. It's more flexible and more protective when one part of a claim is unusually large, which is why higher-limit and commercial auto policies favour it. The trade-off is usually a somewhat higher premium for the added cushion.

plain: Coverage for vehicles a business owns or uses, broader than a personal auto policy.
snappy: Coverage for vehicles used in business, carrying higher limits and covering uses a personal auto policy excludes.
detail: A personal auto policy excludes most business use, so companies — from a plumber's van to a delivery fleet — buy commercial auto insurance with higher liability limits, coverage for employees driving, and for hired or non-owned vehicles. It costs more because business driving means more miles and exposure. The line between personal and commercial use trips up gig workers and small-business owners who assume their personal policy covers work driving.

plain: Coverage for money and property a business loses to theft, fraud, forgery, or computer scams.
snappy: Coverage protecting businesses against losses from employee theft, robbery, forgery, fraud, and funds-transfer scams.
detail: Commercial crime insurance covers the many ways money goes missing: employee theft, burglary and robbery, forged cheques, counterfeit currency, and increasingly the fraudulent funds transfers and social-engineering scams that trick staff into wiring money to crooks. Employee dishonesty, handled by a fidelity bond, is its core, but the policy reaches outside threats too. Businesses that move cash or have many hands on the books treat it as essential, since standard property policies exclude most theft of money.

plain: The core business liability policy — it pays when your operations, products, or premises injure someone or damage their property.
snappy: A standard business policy covering bodily injury, property damage, and advertising-related claims arising from a company's operations, premises, and products.
detail: Commercial general liability is the foundation of nearly every business's insurance program. It answers three exposures: injury or property damage from your operations or premises, completed operations from work you've already finished, and personal and advertising injury such as libel or slander. It carries a per-occurrence limit and an annual aggregate, and the duty to defend often matters more than the payout. Proof you carry it, by certificate of insurance, is a routine condition of winning contracts.

plain: Insurance sold to businesses and organizations, as opposed to coverage sold to individuals and families.
snappy: The category of insurance covering businesses and institutions, spanning property, liability, workers' comp, and specialty risks.
detail: Commercial lines is the half of the industry that insures organizations rather than households: a bakery's property and liability, a trucking fleet's auto cover, a hospital's malpractice, a factory's workers' comp. The coverages are negotiated, underwritten case by case, and often bundled into package policies. It contrasts with personal lines — the standardized home, auto, and life products sold to individuals — and it's where the largest and most specialized risks live.

plain: A build-your-own business policy that bolts several coverages together for larger or unusual companies.
snappy: A modular commercial policy assembling two or more coverage parts — property, liability, auto, crime — under one contract.
detail: A commercial package policy is the customizable alternative to a pre-set businessowners policy: an agent assembles the coverage parts a particular company needs — property, general liability, commercial auto, crime, inland marine — into a single contract with one renewal date and often a package discount. It suits larger or higher-risk businesses whose exposures don't fit the tidy bundle a businessowners policy offers, giving underwriters room to tailor each line.

plain: Insurance for the buildings, equipment, and inventory a business owns or rents.
snappy: Coverage for a business's physical assets — buildings, contents, stock, and equipment — against fire, theft, and other listed perils.
detail: Commercial property insurance is the business cousin of a homeowners policy: it pays to repair or replace the building, machinery, furniture, and inventory after a fire, storm, theft, or other covered peril. It can be written on a named-perils or open-perils basis and settles on replacement cost or actual cash value. Paired with business income coverage, it protects not just the assets but the earnings they generate, and it anchors most commercial package policies.

plain: Extra liability coverage that stacks on top of a business's auto, general liability, and employers liability limits.
snappy: A policy adding liability limits above a business's underlying coverages and dropping down when one is exhausted.
detail: A commercial umbrella sits above a business's primary liability policies — general liability, commercial auto, employers liability — adding a layer, often in millions, once those underlying limits are spent. It can also drop down to cover some claims the primary policies exclude. A single catastrophic event, a multi-vehicle crash or a fire that injures many, can blow through a $1 million primary limit, and the umbrella is the cheap insurance against that worst day.

plain: Pricing that charges everyone in an area the same, instead of charging sick people more.
snappy: Setting premiums by geography and a few allowed factors rather than individual health, so the sick aren't priced out.
detail: Under the ACA's modified community rating, insurers can vary individual premiums only by area, age, family size, and tobacco use — not by health or gender. It spreads the cost of the sick across the whole pool, the flip side of guaranteed issue. Pure community rating would charge literally everyone the same; the modified version keeps age bands. It's why a 20-year-old and a 60-year-old pay different but capped-ratio premiums.

plain: A rule that splits blame for a crash by percentage, reducing payouts by your own share of fault.
snappy: A liability rule apportioning damages by each party's percentage of fault rather than barring a partly-at-fault claimant.
detail: Under comparative negligence, if you're found 30% at fault for a crash, you recover 70% of your damages. It softens the old all-or-nothing contributory-negligence rule that barred any recovery for a plaintiff even slightly to blame. States vary: "pure" comparative lets you recover even at 99% fault, while "modified" versions cut you off at 50% or 51%. Adjusters and courts haggle over these percentages in nearly every disputed auto claim.

plain: Money a court awards to put an injured person back where they were — medical bills, lost wages, pain.
snappy: Damages intended to reimburse a plaintiff for actual losses, both economic (bills, lost income) and non-economic (pain, suffering).
detail: Compensatory damages are the make-whole part of a liability award: they reimburse what the harm actually cost. Economic damages cover the countable losses — medical bills, lost wages, repair costs — while non-economic damages put a number on pain, suffering, and lost enjoyment of life. They're what a liability policy is built to pay, distinct from punitive damages meant to punish. Sizing them is the core of every settlement negotiation and jury verdict.

plain: Business coverage for harm caused by work you already finished — like a deck that collapses months after you built it.
snappy: The general liability coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from a contractor's work after it is finished and handed over.
detail: Completed operations covers the long tail of a contractor's risk: the wiring that sparks a fire a year after the job, the deck that gives way once you've left the site. Because the harm surfaces after the work is done, claims can arrive long after the project closed, so this part of a general liability policy is where occurrence-based coverage earns its keep. Tradespeople watch it closely, since dropping the policy can leave finished jobs unprotected.

plain: Car insurance for damage that isn't a crash — theft, fire, hail, vandalism, or hitting a deer.
snappy: First-party coverage paying for non-collision losses to the covered vehicle: theft, fire, weather, vandalism, animal strikes.
detail: Comprehensive coverage — sometimes called "other than collision" — handles the things that happen to a parked or driving car short of a crash: theft, a cracked windshield, hail, flood, fire, vandalism, or a deer in the road. It carries its own deductible and, like collision coverage, is required by lenders. Together the two make up "full coverage." In hail- and flood-prone regions, comprehensive claims drive much of the premium.

plain: The fine-print duties you must meet — like reporting a loss promptly — or the insurer can refuse to pay.
snappy: Policy provisions setting out the duties and procedures the insured must follow for coverage to apply.
detail: Notify the insurer promptly, cooperate with the investigation, protect property from further damage, submit a proof of loss on time — these strings are attached to every grant of coverage. Break a material one and the insurer may deny an otherwise valid claim. This section is also where you find how disputes are resolved, how other insurance is coordinated, and the right of the insurer to inspect or audit.

plain: The first two years of a life policy, when the insurer can still investigate and void it for lies on the application.
snappy: An initial period, usually two years, during which an insurer may rescind a policy for misstatements; after it, claims stand.
detail: During the contestability period — typically the first two years — a life insurer can review the application after a death claim and rescind the policy for material misrepresentation, refunding premiums instead of paying. Once it passes, the incontestability clause locks the policy in: even a discovered misstatement can no longer undo it, except for outright fraud in some states. It's why deaths soon after a policy is issued draw extra scrutiny.

plain: The backup who collects the life insurance if your first-choice beneficiary has already died.
snappy: A beneficiary who receives policy proceeds only if every primary beneficiary has died before the insured.
detail: Naming a contingent beneficiary is the safety net: if your primary beneficiary dies before you and you never update the form, the proceeds go to the contingent rather than into your estate, where probate and creditors can reach them. Spouses are often primary, children contingent. Keeping both designations current after deaths, divorces, and births is the single most overlooked piece of life insurance housekeeping.

plain: Coverage for liability you take on by signing a contract, not liability the law would have imposed anyway.
snappy: The general liability coverage for liability a policyholder assumes under contract, such as a hold harmless or indemnification clause.
detail: Contractual liability is how a general liability policy responds when you've promised, in a signed agreement, to shoulder another party's exposure. Construction and vendor contracts are full of these assumptions, and without the coverage a hold harmless promise could fall outside the policy. Insurers cover liability assumed under an insured contract — a defined category — while watching for over-broad clauses that pile on risk the underwriter never priced.

plain: A term life policy you can later switch to permanent coverage without a new medical exam.
snappy: A term policy with an option to convert to permanent insurance without re-proving insurability, within a set window.
detail: A convertible term policy carries a valuable option: within a stated period you can convert some or all of it to permanent coverage at standard rates without a new medical exam, even if your health has since collapsed. It protects against becoming uninsurable. Buyers who expect their needs or finances to change later pay a little more for term that converts, locking in future access to permanent insurance.

plain: The rules that decide which plan pays first when you're covered by two of them.
snappy: Rules determining the order in which two or more health plans pay when a person is covered by more than one.
detail: When a child is on both parents' plans, or a worker has employer coverage plus a spouse's, coordination of benefits sets which plan is primary and pays first and which is secondary and picks up the remainder. The goal is to stop double payment while making sure the patient isn't shortchanged. The "birthday rule" — the parent whose birthday falls earlier in the year pays first — is the classic tiebreaker for kids.

plain: A flat fee — say $25 — you hand over at the doctor or pharmacy, with insurance covering the rest.
snappy: A fixed dollar amount the insured pays for a covered health service, separate from the deductible and coinsurance.
detail: A $30 copay for a primary-care visit or $10 for a generic drug is predictable, which is why plans use copays for routine care — you know the cost before you walk in. Copays may or may not count toward your deductible, but they do count toward the out-of-pocket maximum. You'll see them printed on your insurance card next to the network type so the front desk knows what to collect.

plain: Extra help on a marketplace plan that shrinks your deductible and copays if your income is low enough.
snappy: An ACA subsidy that lowers deductibles, copays, and the out-of-pocket maximum for lower-income silver-plan enrollees.
detail: On top of the premium tax credit, a cost-sharing reduction quietly upgrades a silver marketplace plan for lower-income buyers — slashing the deductible, copays, and out-of-pocket maximum so the plan pays a bigger share of each bill. You must pick a silver plan to get it. Many eligible people miss out by choosing bronze for the lower premium, not realising they're leaving this help on the table.

plain: The protection your policy actually provides — the specific losses it promises to pay for.
snappy: The scope of protection a policy grants: which perils, people, and property it pays for, up to stated limits.
detail: Coverage is what you're buying. A homeowners policy might pay for fire and theft but not flood; an auto policy splits protection into liability, collision, and comprehensive. Agents talk about "gaps in coverage" when a real-world loss falls outside every section of the policy. Reading which coverages you have — and at what limit — is the difference between a paid claim and an unpleasant surprise.

plain: A score from your credit history that many insurers use to help set your premium.
snappy: A score derived from credit data that insurers use, where allowed, as a predictor of future claims and pricing.
detail: Insurers in most states use a credit-based insurance score — built from your credit history but distinct from a lending credit score — because it statistically predicts claims. Better credit often means a lower premium, a practice critics call unfair to lower-income drivers and that a few states (California, Hawaii, Massachusetts) ban for auto. It's a quiet but powerful factor that surprises drivers who don't realise credit affects their car insurance.

plain: A policy that pays a lump sum of cash if you're diagnosed with a serious illness like cancer or a heart attack.
snappy: Supplemental coverage paying a fixed cash benefit on diagnosis of a covered serious illness, used however the insured wishes.
detail: Critical illness insurance pays a tax-free lump sum — say $20,000 — on diagnosis of a covered condition such as cancer, heart attack, or stroke, no matter your medical bills. The cash can cover the deductible, lost income, or travel for treatment. Sold as a cheap voluntary benefit at work, it plugs gaps a high-deductible health plan leaves. Critics note the narrow list of covered conditions and the fine print on what counts.

plain: Coverage for the costs of a data breach or cyberattack — from notifying customers to paying ransom and lawsuits.
snappy: Coverage for losses from data breaches and cyber incidents, including response costs, liability to affected parties, and business interruption.
detail: Cyber liability insurance answers the modern breach: it funds forensic investigation, customer notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines, lawsuits from exposed individuals, and increasingly the ransom and downtime of an attack. Standard property and general liability policies were never built for digital harm, so this stand-alone line filled the gap and grew fast. Underwriters now demand real security controls — multi-factor login, backups, employee training — before they'll quote, making the coverage a lever for better security.

plain: The money a life insurance policy pays out when the insured person dies.
snappy: The sum a life insurer pays beneficiaries when the insured dies, generally free of federal income tax.
detail: The death benefit is the whole point of life insurance — the face amount paid to beneficiaries when the insured dies, usually income-tax-free. On permanent policies it can be the face amount alone or the face amount plus accumulated cash value, depending on the option chosen. Riders like accelerated death benefit let a terminally ill insured tap part of it early. Annuities also carry a death benefit for money left at death.

plain: The front page of your policy listing who's covered, for what, and for how much.
snappy: The summary page of the policy stating the named insured, coverages, limits, deductibles, premium, and policy period.
detail: The declarations page — "the dec page" — is the cheat sheet agents pull up first. It personalises the standard policy form with your name, address, vehicle or building, the coverages you bought, their limits and deductibles, and the premium. A lender asking for "proof of insurance" usually wants this page. If a fact here is wrong, the policy may not respond the way you expect when you file a claim.

plain: The slice of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest.
snappy: A fixed amount the insured absorbs on each claim before coverage kicks in; higher deductibles mean lower premiums.
detail: If your car repair costs $3,000 and your deductible is $500, you pay $500 and the insurer pays $2,500. It keeps small nuisance claims off the books and gives you a reason to drive carefully. Choosing a higher figure lowers your premium because you're shouldering more of the risk. Health, auto, and homeowners policies all use this tool, though health plans layer on coinsurance and copays too.

plain: A policy where the lawyers' fees come out of the same pot as the settlement — so defence shrinks what's left to pay claims.
snappy: A liability policy structure in which the cost of legal defence is deducted from, rather than added on top of, the policy limit.
detail: Most liability policies pay defence costs in addition to the limit, but defence-within-limits policies — common in professional and management liability — fold legal fees into the same bucket as any settlement. A long, expensive defence can erode the limit before a dollar reaches the claimant, which is why these are nicknamed burning or eroding limits. Buyers of this structure size their limits with the cost of fighting a claim, not just losing it, firmly in mind.

plain: The cleared buffer around a home in wildfire country that insurers increasingly require for coverage.
snappy: A maintained, vegetation-cleared zone around a structure reducing wildfire risk, often required for coverage in fire-prone areas.
detail: In wildfire-prone regions, defensible space — clearing brush, trimming trees, and using fire-resistant materials in a buffer around the house — is the difference between a home that survives an ember storm and one that doesn't. Insurers now inspect for it and may decline, non-renew, or surcharge homes without it. As wildfire losses mount, this once-voluntary practice has become a condition of staying insurable in much of the West.

plain: An annuity that grows your money tax-deferred for years before income payments begin.
snappy: An annuity with an accumulation phase that builds value tax-deferred, with income or withdrawals starting at a later date.
detail: A deferred annuity has two lives: an accumulation phase where the money grows tax-deferred, then a payout phase that can begin years later through annuitization or withdrawals. Fixed, indexed, and variable versions differ by how the value grows. Savers use them as a tax-deferred supplement to retirement accounts, but surrender charges lock the money up early on and gains are taxed as ordinary income when taken.

plain: A plan that helps pay for cleanings, fillings, and bigger dental work, usually with a low annual cap.
snappy: Coverage for dental care, typically with full preventive cleanings but a low annual maximum on major work.
detail: Dental insurance works differently from medical: it usually covers preventive cleanings fully, basic work like fillings at a share, and major work like crowns at half — all under a low annual maximum, often around $1,500. Hit the cap and you pay the rest yourself. It's commonly sold as a standalone or employer add-on, and the modest limits mean it cushions routine care more than it protects against catastrophe.

plain: The drop in an item's value as it ages and wears — subtracted when a policy pays actual cash value.
snappy: The decline in property value from age, wear, and obsolescence, deducted from replacement cost to reach actual cash value.
detail: A claims adjuster paying actual cash value depreciates your loss: a sofa half through its useful life is paid at roughly half its new price. The recoverable portion is what a replacement-cost policy holds back and releases once you rebuild. Arguments over how fast a roof or appliance wears are among the most common sticking points in property claims.

plain: The drop in a car's resale worth after it's been in an accident, even once perfectly repaired.
snappy: The loss in a vehicle's market value after a repaired accident, sometimes recoverable as a claim against the at-fault driver.
detail: Even a flawless repair can't erase a crash from a car's history, so a repaired vehicle sells for less — that gap is diminished value. In many states you can claim it from the at-fault driver's insurer, though your own insurer usually won't pay it on a first-party claim. Proving the amount takes an appraisal. It surprises owners who assumed a good repair made them whole.

plain: Coverage that protects a company's board and executives personally when they're sued over how they ran the business.
snappy: Coverage for the personal liability of directors and officers arising from decisions made in their corporate roles.
detail: Directors and officers insurance shields the people who steer a company from claims that they breached their duties — shareholders alleging a bad merger, regulators questioning disclosures, employees or competitors suing the leadership. It protects executives' personal assets when the company can't or won't indemnify them, and reimburses the company when it does. Any business seeking outside investors or a capable board effectively must carry it, since few directors will serve without the protection.

plain: Income protection that pays you part of your paycheck if illness or injury keeps you from working.
snappy: Coverage replacing a portion of earned income when illness or injury prevents the insured from working.
detail: Disability insurance protects the asset most people forget — their ability to earn. Short-term policies cover weeks to months; long-term ones can pay to retirement age, typically replacing 50–70% of income after an elimination period. Employers often provide a base layer, which workers supplement individually. It matters most for those whose savings couldn't survive a year off work, and the definition of "disabled" in the policy decides whether a claim pays.

plain: A yearly payment some life policies return to owners when the insurer does better than expected.
snappy: A return of surplus paid to owners of a participating policy when the insurer does better than its conservative pricing assumed.
detail: A mutual insurer prices participating whole life conservatively, then returns the surplus as an annual dividend when claims, expenses, and investments come in better than assumed. It isn't guaranteed. Owners can take it as cash, use it to cut premiums, or buy paid-up additions that grow the death benefit and cash value. Dividends are treated as a return of premium for tax purposes until they exceed what you paid in.

plain: Homeowner coverage for injuries your dog causes — a major and rising share of liability claims.
snappy: Liability coverage paying for injuries caused by a dog the policyholder owns, a leading driver of homeowners liability claims.
detail: Dog bites and related injuries are one of the largest categories of homeowners liability claims, costing insurers over a billion dollars a year. Personal liability coverage typically pays, but insurers respond by surcharging, excluding certain breeds, or refusing to cover a dog with a bite history. A serious bite claim can exhaust the standard liability limit, another reason owners with dogs are urged to carry an umbrella policy.

plain: Driving drunk or drugged — a conviction that sends car insurance costs soaring or gets you dropped.
snappy: A conviction for operating a vehicle while impaired, treated by insurers as a major red flag that sharply raises premiums.
detail: A DUI is among the costliest marks on a driving record. After a conviction, insurers surcharge heavily — often doubling or tripling the premium — may refuse to renew, and frequently require an SR-22 filing for years, pushing many drivers into the nonstandard market. The violation typically affects rates for three to five years or longer. It's the offense that most reliably turns a standard driver into a high-risk one.

plain: The legal obligation to act with reasonable caution so you don't foreseeably harm others.
snappy: A legal obligation requiring a person or business to exercise reasonable care to avoid foreseeably harming others.
detail: Duty of care is the first question in any negligence claim: did the defendant owe the plaintiff an obligation to be careful? A shopkeeper owes it to customers, a driver to others on the road, a doctor to patients. Once a duty exists, the law measures whether it was breached. Businesses manage their duty of care through safety programs and signage, and their liability insurance stands behind them when, despite the effort, someone is harmed.

plain: The promise by your insurer to hire and pay lawyers to fight a covered lawsuit against you.
snappy: An obligation on a liability insurer to provide and fund a legal defence for claims that potentially fall within coverage.
detail: The duty to defend is broader than the duty to pay: an insurer must defend a lawsuit if any allegation might be covered, even if it later proves it owes nothing. Defence costs often dwarf the eventual settlement, so this promise is a big part of a liability policy's value. Refuse to defend wrongly and the insurer risks a bad-faith judgment far above the policy limit.

plain: The part of a home policy that pays to rebuild the house itself after a covered disaster.
snappy: The homeowners coverage paying to repair or rebuild the physical structure of the home, up to its limit.
detail: Dwelling coverage is the core of a homeowners policy, paying to rebuild the house and attached structures after a fire, storm, or other covered peril. Its limit should reflect the cost to rebuild, not the market price or mortgage balance, which is why underinsurance is so common. Other coverages (personal property, liability) are often set as a percentage of this number, so getting it right matters most.

plain: The slice of premium an insurer has truly earned because that part of the coverage period has already passed.
snappy: The portion of a prepaid premium an insurer has earned as time elapses, recognised as revenue over the policy period.
detail: Pay $1,200 for a year of cover and after one month the insurer has earned $100; the other $1,100 is unearned premium it would refund if you cancelled. Insurers report earned premium as revenue and measure their loss ratio against it. The distinction matters at cancellation and in accounting, where booking premium before it's earned overstates how well a carrier is really doing.

plain: Separate coverage for quake damage, which standard home policies exclude.
snappy: A separate policy or endorsement covering earthquake damage, with high percentage deductibles, excluded from standard cover.
detail: Standard homeowners policies exclude earthquakes, so those in seismic zones buy earthquake insurance separately, often through a state-run earthquake pool. Deductibles are steep — commonly 10% to 25% of the coverage limit — so it protects against catastrophic collapse rather than cracked plaster. Low take-up means many quake-zone homeowners are unknowingly exposed, a gap regulators and insurers keep trying to close.

plain: The day your coverage switches on.
snappy: The calendar date coverage under a policy begins; losses before it are not covered even if the premium is paid.
detail: Coverage doesn't exist until the effective date, which is why buyers time it to the moment they take the car keys or close on a house. Backdating is generally barred to stop people insuring a loss that already happened. Lenders and motor-vehicle offices check it against the purchase to be sure there was never an uninsured gap.

plain: A surveyor's document showing how high a home sits relative to flood levels, used to price flood coverage.
snappy: A certified document recording a building's elevation against the base flood level, used to rate flood insurance.
detail: An elevation certificate, prepared by a licensed surveyor, records how high a building's lowest floor sits relative to the base flood elevation FEMA has mapped. The higher above the flood line, the lower the flood insurance premium — so for homes in a flood zone the certificate can save or cost thousands a year. Owners obtain one to challenge a high rate or a zone designation they believe is wrong.

plain: The waiting stretch after you become disabled before benefit payments start.
snappy: The time between a disability or claim trigger and the start of benefit payments, functioning like a time-based deductible.
detail: On a disability policy, the elimination period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits begin — often 90 days, sometimes longer for long-term coverage. A longer elimination period lowers the premium, the same trade-off as a higher deductible. It exists to keep small, short claims off the insurer and to make you self-insure the first stretch. Long-term care policies use the same waiting-period mechanism.

plain: The part of workers' comp that covers an employer sued over a workplace injury beyond the no-fault benefits.
snappy: Coverage protecting employers against lawsuits arising from work-related injuries that fall outside no-fault workers' comp benefits.
detail: Workers' comp has two parts. The first pays statutory benefits to injured workers; employers liability is the second, covering lawsuits that slip past the exclusive remedy — a spouse's claim, a third party seeking contribution, or injury alleged to be the employer's gross fault. It carries its own limits, often shown as three figures. Together the two parts let workers' comp both pay benefits automatically and defend the employer when someone sues anyway.

plain: Coverage for being sued by an employee — over discrimination, harassment, or wrongful firing.
snappy: Coverage protecting employers against claims by workers alleging discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, or retaliation.
detail: Employment practices liability covers the lawsuits that come from inside: a fired worker alleging discrimination, an employee claiming harassment, a candidate citing a biased hiring process. General liability and workers' comp both exclude these, leaving a gap this coverage fills, including the legal defence that often dwarfs the settlement. As workplace claims have multiplied, it's moved from a large-employer luxury to standard protection for businesses of almost any size.

plain: An add-on that changes your policy — adding, removing, or tweaking what's covered.
snappy: A written amendment to a policy that adds, restricts, or modifies coverage; also called a rider in life and health.
detail: Add a home office, schedule a wedding ring, or buy back flood coverage and the insurer issues an endorsement that becomes part of the contract. It can expand coverage or quietly cut it, so reading the change at renewal matters. Standardised industry forms mean the same numbered amendment carries identical wording across many carriers, which is why agents quote them by code.

plain: A middle-ground health plan: no referrals needed, but it only pays for its own network of doctors.
snappy: A plan that, like a PPO, needs no referrals but, like an HMO, covers only in-network care outside emergencies.
detail: An EPO splits the difference between HMO and PPO. You don't need a primary care physician or referrals to see specialists, but step outside the network for anything but an emergency and you pay the full bill. Premiums sit between an HMO and a PPO. It suits people who want freedom from referrals but can live within a defined network to keep costs down.

plain: Home coverage for sudden mechanical or electrical failure of major systems — heating and cooling, the water heater, appliances.
snappy: An endorsement covering sudden breakdown of home systems and appliances from mechanical or electrical failure, not wear.
detail: Standard homeowners policies cover a furnace destroyed by fire but not one that simply burns out — that's where equipment breakdown coverage helps, paying to repair or replace home systems and appliances after a sudden mechanical or electrical failure or a power surge. It's a cheap endorsement, not a maintenance plan: gradual wear and neglect are still excluded. Owners confuse it with a home warranty, which is a service contract, not insurance.

plain: The 1974 federal law that governs most employer-sponsored health and retirement benefits.
snappy: The federal law setting standards for private-sector benefit plans and pre-empting state regulation of self-funded plans.
detail: ERISA sets the ground rules for employer health and pension plans — disclosure, fiduciary duty, and an appeals process for denied claims. Crucially, it pre-empts state insurance law for self-funded plans, which is why a big employer's coverage can skip state mandates. When a denied claim heads to federal court rather than a state insurance commissioner, ERISA is the reason. It shapes the legal backdrop of nearly all job-based benefits.

plain: The ten categories of care every marketplace plan must cover — from hospital stays to maternity to mental health.
snappy: Ten benefit categories the ACA requires individual and small-group plans to cover, from emergency care to prescriptions.
detail: Before the ACA, plans could skip maternity care or prescription drugs to cut premiums. Essential health benefits force every individual and small-group plan to cover ten categories — hospitalisation, emergency care, maternity, mental health, prescriptions, preventive care, and more — with no annual or lifetime dollar limits. The rule is why a cheap plan can't simply carve out the expensive things you might actually need.

plain: Short-term coverage for a wedding, festival, or conference against cancellation and accidents.
snappy: Temporary coverage for a one-off event, covering cancellation, liability for injuries, and sometimes weather or vendor failure.
detail: Event insurance is liability and cancellation cover bought for a single occasion — a wedding, concert, trade show, or charity gala. The liability side pays if a guest is hurt or property is damaged, and venues increasingly require it before they'll book. The cancellation side refunds deposits if a storm, illness, or vendor failure scuttles the day. It packages, for a few days, the protections a permanent business would carry year-round.

plain: Coverage that only pays after an underlying policy limit is used up.
snappy: A policy that responds above a stated attachment point, paying only once the underlying coverage is exhausted.
detail: A factory needing $50 million of liability cover stacks layers: a primary policy to $5 million, then excess policies for each band above. Each excess insurer pays only when the layer beneath is spent, so its premium is lower per dollar of limit. Towers of excess insurance are how big risks get covered when no single carrier wants the whole exposure.

plain: A household member specifically left off your policy, whose driving the insurer won't cover.
snappy: A named person barred from coverage under a policy, used to keep a high-risk household member from raising the premium.
detail: Naming an excluded driver lets you keep a high-risk household member — a teen with violations, a relative with a DUI — off your policy so their record doesn't inflate your premium. The catch: if that person drives your car and crashes, there's no coverage at all, leaving you personally liable. It's a deliberate trade some families make, and it must be signed and documented to be valid.

plain: A loss your policy specifically refuses to cover, listed in black and white.
snappy: A clause carving a peril, property, or circumstance out of coverage; the first place an adjuster looks to deny a claim.
detail: Every policy has exclusions — flood and earthquake on a standard homeowners policy, intentional acts, war, normal wear and tear. They exist to keep premiums affordable and to push uninsurable or specialist risks into separate policies. When a claim is denied, the denial letter cites the exclusion by number. Knowing yours is how you discover you need a flood policy or a separate rider before the loss, not after.

plain: The rule that workers' comp is an injured employee's only path — they get benefits but give up the right to sue.
snappy: The legal doctrine making workers' compensation benefits the sole remedy against an employer for a workplace injury.
detail: Exclusive remedy is the bargain at the heart of workers' compensation: an injured employee receives benefits quickly and without proving fault, and in return gives up the right to sue the employer for more. It shields businesses from open-ended injury verdicts and gives workers certainty. Courts guard the boundary — intentional harm or a missing comp policy can break the shield — but in the ordinary case it keeps workplace injuries inside the comp system rather than the courtroom.

plain: A multiplier on a company's workers'-comp premium that rewards a clean safety record and punishes a bad one.
snappy: A debit or credit applied to workers' compensation premium based on how a company's claim history compares to its industry peers.
detail: The experience modification factor turns a company's claims history into a price knob. A mod of 1.0 is average; below it earns a discount, above it a surcharge, all measured against similar businesses in the same class codes. A 0.85 mod cuts the premium 15%, a 1.25 adds 25%. Because contractors often need a mod under 1.0 to win bids, it gives employers a direct financial reason to drive down workplace injuries.

plain: The day your coverage runs out unless you renew.
snappy: The date coverage under a policy ends; without renewal or extension, the insured is bare from that moment on.
detail: Miss the expiration date without renewing and you're uninsured the next morning, even if you never meant to cancel. Carriers send renewal offers weeks ahead; ignoring them is the most common way people accidentally let coverage drop. Claims-made liability policies make the date doubly important because reporting a claim after expiration — without tail coverage — leaves old work unprotected.

plain: The statement your plan sends after a claim showing what was billed, what it paid, and what you owe.
snappy: A post-claim statement detailing the billed charge, allowed amount, plan payment, and the patient's remaining responsibility.
detail: An explanation of benefits is not a bill — it's the plan's accounting of a processed claim: the provider's charge, the allowed amount, what the plan paid, and what counts toward your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Reading it catches errors and surprise charges before the provider's actual bill arrives. The words "not a bill" are printed at the top precisely because so many people mistake it for one.

plain: How much potential loss an insurer is on the hook for — the size of the bet it took.
snappy: The measure of potential loss an insurer carries, by policy, peril, or region; the base on which premium is calculated.
detail: An insurer measures hurricane exposure as the total it could pay if one storm hit every coastal home it covers. The word also names the rating base — payroll for workers' comp, sales for product liability, square footage for a building — that scales the premium. Managing accumulated exposure in one zip code or one peril is why carriers buy reinsurance and cap how much they'll write in a single area.

plain: Home coverage that adds a cushion — often 25% — above your dwelling limit in case rebuilding costs more.
snappy: An endorsement paying a set percentage above the dwelling limit toward rebuilding, short of a full guarantee.
detail: Extended replacement cost is the common middle ground between a hard policy limit and an open-ended guarantee: it pays up to a set percentage — typically 25% or 50% — over your dwelling coverage limit if rebuilding costs overshoot. It guards against the construction-cost spikes that follow a regional disaster, when everyone rebuilds at once.
