That flexibility cuts both ways — underfund it for years and rising internal costs can drain the cash value and lapse the policy, a problem that has produced lawsuits and surprise premium calls for older policyholders.

plain: Car insurance that prices your premium on how you actually drive, tracked by an app or device.
snappy: Auto coverage that sets premiums from telematics data on mileage, braking, speed, and time of day rather than proxies alone.
detail: Usage-based insurance uses a plug-in device or phone app to track how, when, and how far you drive — hard braking, speeding, late-night trips, total mileage — and prices the premium accordingly. Safe drivers can save; aggressive ones may pay more or lose the discount. Marketed as fairer than traditional rating, it raises privacy questions about who sees your driving data and how long it's kept.

plain: The plan's process of checking whether the care you're getting is necessary and covered.
snappy: A managed-care process evaluating the medical necessity and appropriateness of services before, during, or after care.
detail: Utilization review is how a plan decides whether to pay: it judges medical necessity before treatment (prior authorization), during a hospital stay (concurrent review), or after the fact (retrospective review). Done well it curbs waste; done badly it delays needed care and frustrates doctors. It's the engine behind most coverage denials, and the appeals process exists to challenge it when a reviewer says no.

plain: The duty of both sides to deal honestly and hide nothing important when an insurance contract is made.
snappy: The doctrine that insurer and insured must each disclose all material facts honestly when forming the contract.
detail: Insurance leans on this higher duty of candour because the insured knows facts the insurer can't easily check — your health, your driving, the wiring in your warehouse. Conceal or misstate something material and the insurer may rescind the policy. The doctrine also binds the insurer to deal fairly, the seed of the bad-faith claims that punish carriers who deny coverage without reason.

plain: Special coverage for an empty house, which standard policies stop covering after it sits unoccupied too long.
snappy: Coverage for an unoccupied dwelling, since standard policies restrict or void coverage once a home is vacant beyond a set period.
detail: Standard homeowners policies quietly cut off coverage once a house sits vacant — often after 30 or 60 days — because empty homes invite vandalism, undetected leaks, and fire. Vacant home insurance fills that gap during a renovation, a slow sale, or a probate, at a higher premium reflecting the added risk. Owners caught unaware after an empty house is damaged learn the vacancy exclusion the hard way.

plain: Paying doctors and hospitals for keeping patients healthy and getting good results, not just for doing more.
snappy: Payment models tying provider reimbursement to quality, outcomes, and cost rather than the volume of services.
detail: Value-based care rewires the incentive of fee-for-service: providers are paid partly on outcomes, patient satisfaction, and holding down total cost, often through accountable care organisations or capitation. Medicare drives the shift with programs that bonus or penalise hospitals on readmissions and quality. The promise is better care for less money; the challenge is measuring quality fairly. It's the dominant theme in how payers say they want to pay.

plain: A feature that shrinks your deductible for every year you drive without a claim.
snappy: A benefit reducing the deductible by a set amount for each claim-free year, rewarding safe driving over time.
detail: A vanishing deductible — sometimes a paid add-on — knocks a set amount off your collision deductible for each year you go without an at-fault claim, often down to zero over five years. File a claim and it resets. It rewards loyalty and safe driving, though the feature itself usually carries a small cost, so the real benefit depends on whether you'd otherwise have claimed at all.

plain: An annuity whose value rises and falls with investments you choose, with optional guarantees bolted on.
snappy: A deferred annuity whose value tracks invested subaccounts, often sold with costly guaranteed-income or death-benefit riders.
detail: A variable annuity invests your money in subaccounts like mutual funds, so growth — and loss — follows the market. Insurers attach optional living-benefit riders guaranteeing minimum income or withdrawals for a fee, the main selling point and the main cost. Regulated as securities and sold with a prospectus, they draw scrutiny for layered fees and complexity. They suit buyers wanting market exposure with a guaranteed income floor.

plain: Permanent life insurance whose cash value you invest in funds — with the upside and the risk that brings.
snappy: Permanent life insurance whose cash value is invested in subaccounts chosen by the policyholder, who bears market risk.
detail: Variable life lets you steer the cash value into stock and bond subaccounts, so good markets grow it faster than whole life — and bad markets can shrink it. Because it carries investment risk, it's regulated as a security and sold with a prospectus. The death benefit can rise or fall with performance, though most policies guarantee a floor. It suits buyers who want permanent coverage and market exposure in one wrapper.

plain: A life policy combining universal life's flexible premiums with variable life's invested cash value.
snappy: Permanent life insurance merging adjustable premiums and death benefit with investment subaccounts the policyholder picks.
detail: Variable universal life is the most flexible — and most complex — permanent policy: you adjust premiums and death benefit like universal life and invest the cash value in subaccounts like variable life. The upside is growth and control; the risk is that poor returns or underfunding can collapse the policy. Sold with a prospectus as a security, it appeals to affluent buyers comfortable managing an investment inside their insurance.

plain: Selling your life insurance policy for cash while terminally ill, so a buyer collects the death benefit later.
snappy: The sale of a terminally ill person's life policy to an investor for a lump sum below the death benefit.
detail: In a viatical settlement, a terminally ill policyholder sells their life insurance to an investor for an immediate lump sum — more than the cash surrender value but less than the death benefit — to fund care or final wishes. The buyer keeps paying premiums and collects the death benefit when the insured dies. Created decades ago for the terminally ill, the practice is regulated to protect vulnerable sellers from lowball offers and fraud.

plain: Being held responsible for someone else's wrongdoing — like an employer answering for an employee's mistake.
snappy: Liability assigned to one party for the wrongful acts of another, most often an employer for an employee acting on the job.
detail: Vicarious liability lets a victim reach a deeper pocket: an employer is held responsible for an employee's negligence committed within the scope of the job, even though the boss did nothing wrong personally. A delivery driver who causes a crash makes the company liable too. It's why businesses carry commercial auto and general liability to cover their staff's acts, and why the question of whether someone was on the clock looms so large after an accident.

plain: A low-cost plan covering eye exams, glasses, and contacts.
snappy: A benefit covering routine eye exams and a periodic allowance toward glasses or contact lenses.
detail: Vision insurance is less insurance than a discount plan: for a small premium it covers an annual eye exam and gives an allowance toward frames, lenses, or contacts every year or two. Medical plans cover eye disease and injury; vision plans handle the routine wear of glasses-wearers. Bundled with dental as a voluntary benefit at work, it pays off mainly for those who buy new eyewear regularly.

plain: A rider that keeps your life policy paid up if you become disabled and can't earn an income.
snappy: A rider that suspends premium payments, keeping a policy in force, if the insured becomes totally disabled.
detail: The waiver-of-premium rider is cheap insurance on your insurance: if you become totally disabled and can't work, the insurer pays your premiums for you so the policy doesn't lapse when you can least afford it. Definitions of disability and waiting periods vary, so the fine print matters. It pairs naturally with life and disability coverage as a safeguard against losing protection during a health crisis.

plain: A clause where your insurer gives up its right to chase a named partner for causing a loss it paid.
snappy: A policy endorsement in which the insurer agrees not to pursue recovery from a specific third party after paying a claim.
detail: Normally, after paying a claim an insurer can use subrogation to recover from whoever caused the loss. A waiver of subrogation switches that off for a named party — often demanded in construction and lease contracts so business partners don't end up suing each other through their insurers. The policyholder adds it by endorsement, usually for a small extra premium, to satisfy a contract that says the parties won't shift blame after a covered loss.

plain: An add-on covering damage when water or sewage backs up into your home through drains or a sump pump failure.
snappy: An endorsement covering loss from water or sewage backing up through sewers, drains, or a failed sump pump, normally excluded.
detail: Standard homeowners policies exclude damage from a backed-up sewer or a sump pump that quits during a storm — exactly the soggy basement disaster many owners assume is covered. Water backup coverage is a cheap endorsement that fills the gap, with its own limit. It's distinct from flood insurance, which covers rising external water. Owners with finished basements buy it after the first nasty surprise, or wisely before.

plain: An employer scheme that rewards healthy habits — and can lower your premium for joining.
snappy: An employer initiative encouraging healthy behaviour, sometimes tied to premium discounts or surcharges within legal limits.
detail: Wellness programs offer biometric screenings, smoking-cessation help, or fitness incentives, often dangling a premium discount for participation. Federal rules cap how big the reward or penalty can be and bar discrimination, since a program tied too tightly to health outcomes can shade into the medical underwriting the ACA forbids. Employers pitch them as cost control; the evidence that they actually cut spending is mixed.

plain: Permanent life insurance that covers you for your whole life and slowly builds a savings pot you can borrow against.
snappy: Permanent life insurance with level premiums, a guaranteed death benefit, and a cash value that grows on a fixed schedule.
detail: Whole life lasts your entire life as long as premiums are paid, locks in a level premium, and steadily accumulates guaranteed cash value you can borrow against through a policy loan. It costs far more than term life because part of every premium funds that savings element. Sold heavily for estate planning and forced saving, it's praised for guarantees and criticised for low returns versus buying term and investing the difference.

plain: A separate, often percentage-based deductible that applies only to wind or hail damage.
snappy: A distinct deductible, frequently a percentage of the dwelling limit, applying specifically to wind or hail losses.
detail: In storm-prone regions, insurers carve out a separate wind and hail deductible — often 1% to 5% of the dwelling limit rather than a flat dollar amount — so a roof claim after a hailstorm costs you far more out of pocket than a kitchen fire. On a $400,000 home a 2% wind deductible is $8,000. It lets insurers keep writing in hail country, and it surprises owners who only knew their standard deductible.

plain: Storm-resistant features on a home that earn insurance discounts in hurricane-prone areas.
snappy: Construction features reducing wind damage — roof straps, impact glass — that earn premium credits, verified by inspection.
detail: In hurricane states, a wind mitigation inspection documents features that help a home survive a storm — hurricane straps, a hip roof, impact-resistant windows, a secured roof deck — and each can earn a premium credit. The savings often pay back the inspection many times over, especially in Florida, where insurers must offer the discounts. It rewards owners who build or retrofit for resilience, aligning lower risk with lower cost.

plain: State-mandated coverage that pays an injured employee's medical bills and lost wages, no lawsuit needed.
snappy: Employer-purchased coverage paying medical care and partial wages to workers injured on the job, regardless of fault.
detail: Workers' compensation is the grand bargain of the workplace: employees hurt on the job get prompt medical care and partial wage replacement no matter who was at fault, and in exchange they give up the right to sue their employer — the exclusive remedy. Nearly every state requires employers to carry it, with premiums driven by payroll, job class codes, and an experience modification factor reflecting past claims. It's the most heavily mandated commercial coverage in the country.
